presEras.label: The plebiscites
presEras.blurb: Mobutu put himself to the country three times as the only name on the ballot and was returned with 100%, 98.1% and 99.2%. The 1970 vote reported more ballots than there were registered voters. Green cards meant yes and red meant no, and voters collected them in front of officials.

presEras.label: The transition
presEras.blurb: The first multi-party presidential election in forty-one years was held in 2006 under a United Nations mission, went to a runoff, and was followed by street fighting in Kinshasa between the two candidates' guards. The single-round rule adopted for 2011 let Joseph Kabila win a second term with 49% against a divided field, on a count the opposition and international observers both rejected.

presEras.label: Tshisekedi
presEras.blurb: The 2018 result was the first transfer of power by ballot in Congolese history and also the most disputed: the Catholic Church's observer mission, which had deployed forty thousand monitors, said its own count did not match the published one. Félix Tshisekedi took a second term in December 2023 with 73%, in a vote extended to a second day amid fraud claims and followed by the cancellation of results in two constituencies.

legEras.label: Independence and collapse
legEras.blurb: The Belgian Congo elected a National Assembly in May 1960 with no party close to a majority, and independence lasted ten weeks before the state broke apart. Katanga seceded, Patrice Lumumba was deposed and murdered, and the United Nations fought a war in the south. The 1965 election was held as the country reassembled and was followed within months by Mobutu's coup.

legEras.label: The MPR years
legEras.blurb: The Popular Movement of the Revolution was written into the constitution as the country's only party, and every citizen was a member by birth. Five assemblies were elected on its single list, taking every seat each time. The country was renamed Zaire in 1971.

legEras.label: After the wars
legEras.blurb: Two wars and Mobutu's fall separate the last one-party assembly from the first elected National Assembly of the new republic in 2006. The chamber has grown to five hundred seats and is extraordinarily fragmented: more than a hundred parties won seats in 2011, and the largest party in 2023 held fewer than one seat in seven.
